summary: Describes PASTE, an architecture that lets internet service providers combine differentiated services with traffic engineering. It is a design proposal for provider networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: PASTE is a design for large internet service providers. It groups many traffic flows into a few tunnels, each carrying traffic of one quality level, so that the equipment does not have to track every flow separately. The tunnels are built and repaired with RSVP and can be routed along chosen paths, which lets the provider steer traffic around busy links.

subtitle: An ISP architecture that bundles many traffic flows into a few labelled tunnels so that quality of service and traffic engineering can both be offered at scale.

tldr.problem: A large ISP has far too many traffic flows to keep separate state for each one, so per-flow schemes for differentiated services do not scale. The ISP also wants to move traffic around its own network to avoid congested links.
tldr.mechanism: PASTE groups flows by traffic class and puts each group into an MPLS tunnel called a traffic trunk. Trunks are set up and kept alive with RSVP along explicit routes, and they can be merged and stacked so that the number of tunnels stays small.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and describes a design rather than a protocol. It gives an architecture in which an ISP can offer priority service under an inter-provider agreement, and steer traffic away from congested links, with the number of tunnels growing far more slowly than the number of flows.

facts.label: CoS bits in the MPLS label header

today: RFC 2430 is an Informational memo from October 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes an architecture rather than a protocol, so it sets no standard and no implementation is required to follow it.

sections.title: The Problem PASTE Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 2430 describes the Provider Architecture for Differentiated Services and Traffic Engineering (PASTE), for use by Internet Service Providers. Providing differentiated services in an ISP is a challenge because the sheer number of flows in large ISPs makes the cost of maintaining per-flow state unacceptable. Large ISPs also need the ability to perform traffic engineering, that is, to direct aggregated flows of traffic along specific paths.

PASTE addresses both problems by using Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) to create a scalable traffic management architecture that supports differentiated services. The memo assumes the reader has at least some familiarity with both of these technologies.

Scalability is the primary consideration in any ISP architecture. Solutions whose state grows in proportion to the size of the Internet produce growth rates exceeding Moore's law, so mechanisms with very limited growth rates are strongly preferred. Discussions of differentiated services had frequently resulted in solutions requiring per-flow state or per-flow queuing. As the number of flows in the default-free zone of the Internet scales with the size of the Internet, that growth rate is difficult to support.

Supporting differentiated services is nonetheless a significant benefit for most ISPs. It lets providers offer special services, such as priority bandwidth for mission critical services, to users willing to pay a service premium, under Service Level Agreements. Such an agreement may specify the traffic volume, how the traffic is handled either in an absolute or a relative manner, and the compensation the ISP receives.

The memo also covers what lies beyond a single ISP. Differentiated services are likely to be deployed first across a single ISP, to support something such as one enterprise's Virtual Private Network, but that is only the first wave. Extranets, enterprise VPNs that span ISPs, and industry interconnection networks follow, and because those applications span enterprises and therefore span ISPs, there is a clear need for inter-domain SLAs. The memo describes the technical architecture that would allow such agreements to be created. It covers unicast services only; extensions to support multicast are left to future research.
sections.plainLanguage: A large provider carries so many separate transfers that keeping a record for each one would cost more than the equipment can handle. So the design groups transfers together by the kind of service they need, puts each group in one tunnel, and lets the provider choose which path that tunnel takes. The number of tunnels then grows far more slowly than the number of transfers.

sections.title: Flows, Traffic Classes and Trunks
sections.content:
A flow is a unidirectional stream of packets distributed over time. A flow typically has very fine granularity and reflects a single interchange between hosts, such as a TCP connection. An aggregated flow is a number of flows that share forwarding state and a single resource reservation along a sequence of routers.

MPLS is one mechanism for supporting aggregated flows. Packets are tunnelled by wrapping them in a minimal header, and each such header contains a label that carries both forwarding and resource reservation semantics. MPLS defines mechanisms to install label-based forwarding information along a series of Label Switching Routers to construct a Label Switched Path (LSP). LSPs can also be associated with resource reservation information. One protocol for constructing such LSPs is RSVP, which, used with an Explicit Route Object, can construct an LSP along an explicit route.

For differentiated services, packets are divided into separate traffic classes. The memo discusses three: Best Effort, Priority and Network Control. The exact number of subdivisions within each class is left to be defined.

  • Network Control traffic primarily consists of routing protocols and network management traffic. If it is dropped, routing protocols can fail or flap, resulting in network instability, so Network Control must have very low drop preference. It is generally insensitive to moderate delays and requires a relatively small amount of bandwidth, so a small bandwidth guarantee is sufficient.
  • Priority traffic comes in many flavors depending on the application. Particular flows may require bandwidth guarantees, jitter guarantees, or upper bounds on delay. The memo does not distinguish the subdivisions of Priority traffic and assumes all Priority traffic has an explicit resource reservation.
  • Best Effort is currently the vast majority of traffic in ISPs. It is for the most part delay insensitive and reasonably adaptive to congestion.

When flows are aggregated according to their traffic class and the aggregated flow is placed inside an LSP, the result is called a traffic trunk, or simply a trunk. The traffic class of a packet is orthogonal to the LSP it is on, so many different trunks, each with its own traffic class, may share an LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is one stream of packets in one direction, such as one connection. A trunk is a set of flows of the same kind bundled into one labelled path. Three kinds of traffic are described: ordinary best-effort traffic, priority traffic with a promise attached, and the network's own routing and management traffic, which has to be protected because losing it destabilises the network.

sections.title: Components of the Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture integrates several mechanisms that, used in a coordinated way, achieve the goals.

Traffic classes. It is essential that packets be classified accurately before entering the ISP, and that an ISP device can easily determine the traffic class of a particular packet. The traffic class of MPLS packets can be encoded in the three bits reserved for CoS within the MPLS label header, and traffic classes for IPv4 packets can be classified via the IPv4 ToS byte, possibly within the three precedence bits within that byte. A consistent interpretation of the traffic class, regardless of the bits used, is an important feature of PASTE. It is not overly important to control which packets entering the ISP have a particular traffic class: each Priority packet should involve some economic premium for delivery, so the ISP need not pass judgment on the appropriateness of the traffic class for the application. Network Control traffic entering an ISP must be handled carefully, and its contents must also be carefully authenticated.

Trunks. Trunks decouple the overhead in the infrastructure from the size of the network and the amount of traffic in it: as traffic scales up, the amount of traffic in the trunks increases, not the number of trunks. The worst case is one trunk per traffic class from each entry router to each exit router, which with N routers and C classes of service would be N * (N-1) * C trunks. Trunks with a single exit point that share a common internal path can be merged into a single sink tree. If, when a trunk is being established, it intersects an existing trunk with the same traffic class and the same remaining explicit route, the new trunk can be spliced into the existing trunk at the point of intersection; both incoming trunks perform a standard label switching operation and result in the same outbound label. Since each sink tree touches each router at most once and there is one sink tree per exit router, the result is N * C sink trees. Trunks of different classes that follow the same path can share a label for the shared part, because the traffic class is orthogonal to the path, so the entire topology can be overlaid with N trunks.

If Best Effort trunks and individual Best Effort flows are treated identically there is no need to instantiate any Best Effort trunk following the IGP computed path, because the packets can be forwarded directly without an LSP, although traffic engineering may require Best Effort trunks to be treated differently. Priority trunks must be instantiated, because the end-to-end RSVP packets that support the aggregated Priority flows must be tunnelled. Trunks can also be aggregated with other trunks by adding a new label to the stack of labels for each trunk, bundling them into a single tunnel; traffic class is propagated when the additional label is added, so trunks of different classes may be aggregated. Trunks can be terminated at any point, which deaggregates the traffic and requires sufficient switching capacity at that point to deal with the result. High reliability for a trunk is provided through the use of one or more backup trunks.

RSVP. Its use in PASTE differs from its original design in three ways. RSVP installs state that applies to a collection of flows sharing a common path and a common pool of reserved resources. It installs forwarding state, including label switching information, in addition to resource reservations. And the path that this state is installed along is no longer constrained by destination-based routing. The key factor is the set of mechanisms RSVP provides: a general facility for creating and maintaining distributed reservation state across a mesh of multicast or unicast delivery paths, and a straightforward extensibility mechanism for creating new RSVP objects. RSVP already treats QoS control parameters as opaque data and passes them to the appropriate traffic control modules, and that design extends to explicit route parameters and label binding parameters. An RSVP session in PASTE is also used between pairs of routers acting as the originator and the terminator of a traffic trunk. This consolidates three procedures: establishing forwarding along an explicit route, establishing a label switched path, and RSVP's existing resource reservation procedures. The memo notes the main advantage of the consolidation is that these three tasks are inter-related, so doing them with separate procedures would require additional coordination.

Traffic engineering. Standard IGPs compute the shortest path across the ISP's network based solely on the metric administratively assigned to each link, without taking the loading of each link into account. If the network is not a full mesh of physical links, there may be no obvious way to assign metrics so that no congestion occurs for known traffic patterns. Traffic engineering gives the ISP precise control over the flow of traffic by directing trunks along explicit paths, enumerating an explicit list of the routers in the path. A trunk could be configured manually along the explicit path, with each router along the path given state for forwarding the particular label, or RSVP can be used with an Explicit Route Object so that the first router in the path establishes the trunk.

Resource reservation, inter-provider agreements, and shaping. The mechanism used to communicate the requirements of Priority traffic dynamically is RSVP. The flow specification within RSVP can describe many characteristics of the flow or trunk, and an LSR receiving RSVP information can accept or reject the reservation based on its local policy, likely including constraints on the traffic handling functions the network supports and the aggregate capacity it will provide for Priority traffic. Trunks spanning multiple ISPs are likely to be based on legal agreements, and the memo describes the bilateral agreement between two ISPs as an Inter-Provider SLA, extending the idea of a peering agreement. It may include the types of differentiated services one ISP provides to another, the upper bound on the traffic associated with each service that the ISP is willing to accept, and limits on traffic that originates from a third party ISP and is passed between the signatories. If the expected costs are not symmetric, the parties may agree that one ISP will compensate the other. At the interconnect, shaping and policing facilities are needed so that a trunk of Priority traffic is carried within the agreed traffic characterisation and capacity; a token bucket system implemented on a per-trunk basis is the memo's simplistic example. A multilateral IPS is also possible, though unusual, and the memo notes it may sometimes be simpler to establish aggregated trunks through other ISPs and then contract with customers to aggregate their trunks.
sections.plainLanguage: The pieces are: a class on every packet, so the network knows what it is carrying; trunks, so many packets share one path and one reservation; RSVP, which sets those paths up and keeps them alive; and explicit routes, so the provider can choose the path instead of taking whatever the interior routing protocol picks. Merging trunks that share a path, and stacking labels to bundle several trunks into one, keeps the number of tunnels small.

sections.title: How Traffic Flows Through PASTE
sections.content:
The memo walks through an example: a user makes a telephone call using a Voice over IP service. The call is full duplex, but the data flow in each direction can be considered in a half duplex fashion because the architecture operates symmetrically. The data packets are created at node S and must traverse to node D, and because this is a voice call they are encoded as Priority packets, possibly wanting low jitter and having low drop preference. Initially this is encoded into the precedence bits of the IPv4 ToS byte.

To establish the flow, node S first generates an RSVP PATH message which describes the flow in more detail. The flow might require 3kbps of bandwidth, be insensitive to jitter of less than 50ms, and require a delay of less than 200ms. The message passes through node S's local network and eventually appears in node S's ISP, which the memo calls ISP F.

ISP F has considerable latitude at this point. The requirement on F is to place the flow into a trunk before it exits F's infrastructure. One thing F might do is perform the admission control function at the first hop router, determining whether it has the capacity and capability of carrying the flow across its own infrastructure to an exit router E. If the admission control decision is negative, the first hop router can inform node S using RSVP. Alternately it can propagate the RSVP PATH message along the path to exit router E, which is simply normal operation of RSVP on a differentiated flow.

At exit router E there is a trunk that ISP F maintains that transits ISP X, Y and Z and terminates in ISP L. Based on BGP path information or on out-of-band information, node D is known to be a customer of ISP L. Exit router E matches the flow requirements in the RSVP PATH message to the characteristics of the trunk to ISP L, for example its remaining capacity. Assuming the requirements are compatible, it notes that the flow should be aggregated into the trunk.

To make sure the flow reservation happens end to end, the RSVP PATH message is then encapsulated into the trunk itself, where it is transmitted to ISP L. It eventually reaches the end of the trunk, where it is decapsulated by router U, and PATH messages are then propagated all the way to the ultimate destination D. The end-to-end RSVP RESV messages must be carefully handled by router U: the RESV messages from router U to E must return via a tunnel back to router E. RSVP is also used by exit router E to initialize and maintain the trunk to ISP L. The RSVP messages for this trunk are not placed within the trunk itself, but the end-to-end RSVP messages are.

Data packets created by S follow the flow reservation through ISP F's network and eventually reach router E. At that point they are given an MPLS label and placed in the trunk, and normal MPLS switching propagates the packet across ISP X's network. The same traffic class still applies, because the class encoding is propagated from the precedence bits of the IPv4 header to the CoS bits in the MPLS label. As the packet exits ISP X's network it can be aggregated into another trunk for the express purpose of transiting ISP Y. Label switching brings the packet across ISP Y's network and the aggregated trunk then terminates at a router in ISP Z's network. This router deaggregates the trunk and forwards the resulting trunk towards ISP L. The trunk transits ISP Z and terminates in ISP L at router U, where the data packets are removed from the trunk and forwarded along the path computed by RSVP.

Two trunks are in use in this example. One runs from ISP F through ISPs X, Y and Z and terminates in ISP L. The other aggregated trunk begins in ISP X, transits ISP Y and terminates in ISP Z. The first may be established based on a multilateral agreement between ISPs F, X, Z and L, with ISP X contractually responsible for carriage of the trunk into ISP Z. The tunnel is maintained by ISP F and initialized and maintained through RSVP and an explicit route object that lists ISPs X, Z and L. Within that explicit route, ISP X and ISP L are given as strict hops, so no other ISP may intervene between F and X or between Z and L, but no constraint is placed on the path between X and Z, nor on which router inside L terminates the trunk. The second trunk may be established by a bilateral agreement between ISP X and Y, with ISP Z not involved, and is constrained to terminate on the last hop router within Y's infrastructure. Multiple explicit routes are configured into ISP X's routers so one working route can be selected.

On robustness, the memo notes that in this example there are no single points of failure once the traffic is within ISP F's network. Each trunk has a backup trunk to protect against the failure of the primary trunk, and each trunk can be configured with multiple explicit route objects that terminate at one of several acceptable routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a voice call across four providers. The caller sends a reservation message that describes what the call needs. The first provider checks it has room and puts it into a trunk; the message travels inside the trunk and comes out at the far end, where it continues to the destination. The data packets are labelled and carried along the same trunk, and the acknowledgement messages come back through a separate tunnel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because Priority traffic intrinsically has more value than Best Effort traffic, the ability to inject Priority traffic into a network must be carefully controlled. Signalling concerning Priority traffic also has to be authenticated, because the signalling information is likely to result in specific accounting and eventually in billing for the Priority services. ISPs are cautioned to make sure the Priority traffic they accept is in fact from a known previous hop. The memo notes that this is a simple requirement to fulfil at private peerings, but much more difficult at public interconnects, and that exchanging Priority traffic at public interconnects should be done with great care.

RSVP traffic needs to be authenticated, which the memo says could possibly be done through the use of the Integrity Object.
sections.plainLanguage: Priority traffic is worth more, so two things have to be protected: the traffic itself, which a provider should only accept from a neighbour it knows, and the signalling that reserves capacity for it, because that signalling leads to the bill. Checking the previous hop is easy on a private link and much harder at a public exchange point, where the memo says care is needed.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The memo concludes that PASTE provides a robust, scalable means of deploying differentiated services in the Internet. Scalability comes from aggregating flows into class specific MPLS tunnels. These tunnels, also called trunks, can in turn be aggregated, leading to a hierarchical aggregation of traffic.

Trunk establishment and maintenance is done with RSVP, taking advantage of existing work in differentiated services. Explicit routes within the RSVP signalling structure allow providers to perform traffic engineering by placing trunks on particular links in their network.

The result is an architecture that is sufficient to scale to meet ISP needs, can provide differentiated services on a large scale, supports traffic engineering, and can continue to grow with the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The design scales because many transfers share one tunnel and many tunnels can be bundled into one. Reservations and repairs are handled by RSVP, and the provider chooses the path each tunnel takes. The memo presents this as an architecture that a provider could build on, not as a protocol that anyone has to follow.
